turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Thursday, November 19. I'm Sam.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And I'm Alex. We start in Shenzhen, where 3 leaders sat down together this morning and walked out without a piece of paper.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin met for about an hour and a half on the sidelines of the APEC summit, according to Chinese state media. There was no joint statement and no deal. Trump said the 3 countries are uniquely positioned to cut their nuclear stockpiles, and he tied that pitch to Iran. Xi went further rhetorically, calling for nuclear weapons to be comprehensively prohibited and destroyed.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The silence is the more useful signal. Putin talked up shared interests on Ukraine, and Xi said nothing about Ukraine at all. Beijing will host the photo, but it won't put its name to Moscow's war aims. A separate Trump and Putin bilateral is planned for later today, and Ukraine's allies are due to meet in Berlin right after, which tells you the Europeans expect to be doing damage control on whatever gets said in that room. And arms control with no verification text, after a week of Iranian missiles at US bases, is a talking point, not a framework.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: To Israel, where Benjamin Netanyahu just lost control of the Knesset's gavel. On Tuesday the chamber elected Matan Kahana of Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party as speaker, 66 votes to 52, over Likud's Ofir Katz, replacing Amir Ohana. Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a government, with a possible 2-week extension.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The arithmetic is the story. Those 66 votes included the Joint List and Ra'am, the Arab parties, which Likud is already attacking as relying on terror supporters. Shas and United Torah Judaism stuck with Katz. So Eisenkot has shown he can assemble a majority for a procedural vote, but a governing coalition that leans on Arab parties is exactly what Likud wants to fight the next 3 weeks on. Controlling the speaker's chair still matters: it sets the legislative agenda while the coalition talks run.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And a public-health verdict with a long tail. The Pan American Health Organization ruled on Tuesday that the United States, Mexico and Bolivia have lost measles-elimination status, because the virus has spread continuously for more than 12 months. The US has more than 5,400 confirmed cases this year, the most since 1991, driven largely by an outbreak in Pennsylvania. Mexico's was centred on Chihuahua. All 3 countries now have to submit plans to stop transmission, and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Junior says the US will work to win the status back. It ends 26 years of elimination for the US.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: To US business, and the best quarter Target has had in 5 years. Comparable sales rose 5.6% against 3.8% expected, traffic was up about 5%, and digital comps were up roughly 10%. Earnings were 2 dollars 65 a share, against 1 dollar 51 a year ago, and the full-year earnings guide goes up to 10 dollars 65 to 11 dollars 40, from 9 dollars 90 to 10 dollars 90. The stock rose about 7%.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The mix matters more than the beat. Food and beverage grew 6.6%, beauty grew, and the toys-and-collectibles push, Pokémon cards especially, did a lot of the lifting. Home and apparel, the discretionary categories Target actually makes margin on, stayed weak. So the turnaround is real in traffic, but it's running on necessities and novelty, not on shoppers trading up. And they've set 5 to 6 billion dollars of capex for next year, which is management betting the traffic sticks.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Lowe's sold more and earned less margin. Sales rose 9.3% to about 22.8 billion dollars against 22.4 billion expected, comparable sales were up 1.8% for a sixth straight positive quarter, and adjusted earnings of 3 dollars 10 beat 2 dollars 89. Online sales rose 17.4%. But gross margin fell 124 basis points to 32.9%, and while the full-year sales guide went up to about 92.5 billion, the adjusted operating margin was trimmed to about 11.5%. With Home Depot also guiding cautiously, the read on housing is the same: volume is holding, pricing power isn't.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Internationally, Bank Indonesia surprised the market. It raised its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 6% on Wednesday, the first move since June, taking it to 125 basis points of hikes this year. Most economists had expected a hold.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: This is an emerging-market central bank importing Fed policy. The rupiah was trading around 18,250 to the dollar, the dollar hit a 19-month high on Tuesday, and Bank Indonesia decided it couldn't wait for the Fed to hike first and then defend the currency. It's the same trap Manila is in, and we'll come back to that: when US rates rise, Asia's central banks hike into slowing growth to protect the currency.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And in Europe, final October inflation for the euro area came in at 4%, the highest since September 2023, with energy prices up 20.8% and core at 2.5%. The ECB's Boris Vujčić says a December hike is very likely, barring surprises, at the December 16 and 17 meeting. The Stoxx 600 fell 1% for a third straight loss, with miners down 4.7%, Glencore down 6.1% and copper at a 7-month low. The gap between 4% headline and 2.5% core is the oil shock, and the ECB is signalling it would rather hike into it than wait for second-round effects.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Markets. Stocks were mixed and it's all on the Markets tab. The moves worth reading aloud are in commodities: gold fell more than 3% to around 3,735 dollars an ounce, its lowest since September 2025, and WTI crude dropped about 3% to just under 82 dollars after a surprise build in US inventories.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Gold is the tell. It has been the hedge of choice all year, and it fell 3% on the day the October Fed minutes said almost all officials see further hikes as likely appropriate. Some were open to more than 25 basis points in December if inflation data come in hot, and the minutes flagged AI as both a financial-stability and an inflation risk. Futures now price about a 95% chance of a quarter-point hike on December 9, and Chris Waller is openly arguing for 50. A metal that pays nothing doesn't do well when the real yield on cash keeps rising.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the S&P has now fallen 5 sessions in a row, its longest losing streak since June.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: With an odd internal split. Health insurers and energy dragged the Dow, while the Nasdaq actually rose, helped by AMD up 5%. Nvidia went the other way, down almost 3% on Wednesday after the board ruled out Jensen Huang returning and its quarterly filing was delayed. So the market liked the numbers on Tuesday night and then repriced the governance on Wednesday. That's the pattern this week: the story gets a valuation, and then the details get a discount.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Which brings us to today's main event. Anthropic priced its IPO at 83 dollars a share, above its 70-to-78-dollar range, raising about 81.3 billion dollars. That's the largest IPO on record, ahead of SpaceX's roughly 75 billion, for an initial market value of around 1.08 trillion dollars. It starts trading on Nasdaq today under the ticker ANT.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Pricing above the range at that size says institutional demand is deep. But watch the Hang Seng tech names this morning, which were selling off before the listing, a sign that investors are funding the new trade by trimming the old ones. An 81-billion-dollar float is a liquidity event for the whole AI complex, not just one stock. Also today: Walmart reports, along with jobless claims and the Philadelphia Fed survey.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Our deep dive this morning comes from The Economist's annual look ahead, The World Ahead 2027. The piece is titled Slimming drugs are reshaping consumers, and their behaviour. The argument, as The Economist frames it, is that you already know GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic are bad for junk-food makers, but the effects run much further: bra design is changing, facial fat-grafts are in, and what it calls revenge shopping reaches well beyond food and drink.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Let's rebuild the scale from open data, because the scale is the argument. KFF's survey in March found 12% of American adults currently taking a GLP-1 and 18% who have ever taken one. Use peaks at 22% among people aged 50 to 64. Gallup has weight-loss use roughly doubling, from 5.8% in early 2024 to 12.4%, and the adult obesity rate falling to 37% from a peak near 40% in 2022.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And this year the access problem started to break. The oral version of Wegovy launched in January at 149 dollars a month for the starter dose. Lilly's pill, orforglipron, sold as Foundayo, was approved on April 1 at 149 to 349 dollars self-pay, and Medicare copays dropped to about 50 dollars from July. A weekly injection at 1,000 dollars a month was a niche. A daily pill at 149 dollars is a mass-market consumer product.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: So what does it do to spending? The cleanest study is from Cornell, using Numerator's panel of about 150,000 households, published in the Journal of Marketing Research. Within 6 months of someone starting a GLP-1, household grocery spending falls about 5.5%. In households earning more than 125,000 dollars, it's 8.6%. Chips, sweet bakery and cookies fall between 6.7% and 11%. Circana projects that by 2030, GLP-1 households will account for about 35% of all US food and beverage sales.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That income skew is the detail I'd underline. The drop is biggest among exactly the shoppers packaged-food companies rely on for premium margin.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right, and it extends past food. Circana finds GLP-1 households spend about 7% less a month on alcohol, and 13.5% less on beer. Restaurant visits haven't fallen, they're flat to slightly up, but people order about 1% fewer items, and it's the sides and snacks that go. FTI Consulting puts around 54 billion dollars of restaurant spending at risk by 2030.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Then the categories The Economist is pointing at. On intimates, Circana's data shows bands of 42 and above, and D cups, losing share to smaller sizes, and about 80% of users say they expect to buy new clothes. ThredUp says denim is the top category GLP-1 users buy and resell. And on aesthetics, the American Society of Plastic Surgeons says facial fat grafting was the fastest-growing cosmetic surgery last year, up 39% to more than 34,000 procedures, with GLP-1 patients clustering in facelifts and neck lifts.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the revenge-shopping thesis in one line: the money doesn't disappear, it moves. Less spent on snacks and beer, more on a new wardrobe, a procedure, maybe a trip.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Now the case against. How permanent is any of this?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the real fault line, and it's persistence. For cohorts that started in 2021 to 2023, pharmacy-benefit data showed 60 to 70% quitting within a year, and the Cornell study found that people who stopped saw their spending go back to where it was before. The newer data is better: about 61 to 63% of 2024 starters were still on the drug after a year. So the structural shift depends on a medical question, whether people stay on, not on consumer taste.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the food companies' own numbers are muddier than the headline. Mondelez's chief executive puts the volume hit at 0.5 to 1% over a decade and calls it minimal. PepsiCo says very little impact. Hershey's volumes fell about 10% in its latest filing, but it doesn't blame GLP-1s, and years of price increases are a simpler explanation. Conagra is now putting GLP-1 friendly labels on frozen meals, which is either adaptation or marketing.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: My read is that the companies are underplaying it, and for a reason: no consumer-staples chief executive wants to tell investors their core category is in structural decline. The mismatch is in the data. A 5% household-level drop, concentrated in high-income buyers, spreading because a 149-dollar pill replaced a 1,000-dollar injection, is not minimal. It's a slow re-rating of the snack aisle. The users today skew 50 to 64 and affluent, and the pill is what broadens that.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Economist piece is a reminder that the most consequential consumer technology of the decade might be a molecule, not a chatbot.

segments.raw: SEGMENT FOUR — ENERGY / DATA CENTERS / UTILITIES
segments.label: Energy / Data Centers / Utilities

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Energy, and the regulators are now writing tougher terms than the hyperscalers negotiated. On Tuesday the North Carolina Utilities Commission approved Duke Energy's rate cases, with average annual increases of about 3.4% at Duke Energy Progress and 3.7% at Duke Energy Carolinas, starting January 1. But it went beyond the October 7 settlement that Duke struck with Amazon and Google.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Three things the commission added that the settlement didn't have. First, data centers become their own cost-tracking class, so their costs can't be quietly blended into residential rates. Second, a Stranded Generation Charge, which assigns the cost of new plants built for data centers back to those customers if the load doesn't show up. Third, upfront deposits sized to cover estimated grid-upgrade costs, with 15-year minimum terms reported for loads above 100 megawatts. One commissioner, van der Vaart, partly dissented and resigned, and another wants the tariff to cover every large load, not just data centers.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why does the Stranded Generation Charge matter beyond Carolina?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Because it's a template. The risk in this cycle is that a utility builds gas for a campus that slips or cancels, and ratepayers eat the stranded asset. Settlements with Amazon and Google were negotiated by parties with leverage. A commission-written charge is the regulator saying the risk belongs with the off-taker. Expect it to be copied across the Southeast states doing integrated resource plans, and expect hyperscalers to factor it into site selection.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And Oregon did the same thing this week. The Oregon PUC approved Pacific Power's data-center tariff under the state's POWER Act, creating a class for loads of 20 megawatts and up that pays full cost of service from January 1. Portland General's version raised large data-center rates by 29.7%. With both investor-owned utilities covered, growth around Hillsboro and Prineville likely tilts towards Bonneville and public utility district territory.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Now the federal layer. The grid operators filed their responses to FERC's June show-cause orders on large-load interconnection on Monday, and SPP's is due tomorrow. There's no national standard emerging. CAISO proposed a Flexible Interim Load Interconnection product that lets a load energize before its network upgrades are finished, plus a curtailable service, and it would make generator developers disclose any co-located load. ISO-New England went the other way: large loads must bring their own new capacity, and some are carved out of the installed capacity requirement. NYISO proposes firm and non-firm withdrawal services. And MISO's fast-track for loads of 250 megawatts and up, studied with contracted generation, is opposed by 11 state commissions.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So a developer running a multi-region site search faces 4 different rulebooks.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And 4 different prices for the option to energize early. CAISO and NYISO are effectively pricing non-firm service as a discount product. New England is turning itself into a self-supply market. If you're siting, the question is no longer just where the queue is short, it's which regime lets you trade flexibility for speed.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Which connects to the demand-side risk. Heatmap Pro counts about 260 billion dollars of data-center projects cancelled this year after local opposition, roughly 130 billion of that in the third quarter alone, against 112 billion in 2025 and 16 billion in 2024. Those are announced figures, not dollars spent. Bloomberg tracked 46 local ballot measures and nearly all ended in restrictions, moratoria or bans. Utility Dive's analysis this week is that a slowdown shifts risk onto utility capex plans.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which is precisely why North Carolina and Oregon are front-loading deposits. And note who is building around the gates: Giga Energy signed a 10-year lease worth about 1 billion dollars for a 60-megawatt AI facility called Project Marl in Hunt County, Texas, for an undisclosed AI cloud provider, with power-on targeted for spring 2027. That's roughly 1.67 million dollars per megawatt per year on simple math, and at 60 megawatts it sits under ERCOT's 75-megawatt large-load threshold. Small enough to skip the big-load review is becoming a design choice.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Equipment. Wood Mackenzie puts global gas turbine orders above 100 gigawatts against 60 to 70 gigawatts a year of production capacity. US lead times average about 6 years, and third-quarter pricing was more than 20% above late 2025. Developers are now buying used turbines and converted aero engines, and large power transformers average about 128 weeks.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A secondary market in used turbines trading at a premium puts a mark-to-market floor under every slot reservation in the industry. If a cancelled campus can sell its turbine position at a profit, cancellation risk is partly hedged, which is one reason the build-out bends rather than breaks.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And one from the inbox. Adam Tooze's Chartbook flagged this week that China's solar exports to Southeast Asia jumped almost 60% by capacity in the first 9 months of the year, while exports to Europe fell 11%. Indonesia's President Prabowo is promising to take solar capacity from about 1.5 gigawatts to 100 gigawatts by 2029.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Total Chinese module exports are actually down about 10% this year, to roughly 185 gigawatts, according to industry trackers, so this is a rerouting, not growth. Southeast Asia is turning from a transshipment hub that got around Western tariffs into an end market. Indonesia's first phase is only about 5.2 gigawatts against a roughly 73-billion-dollar programme, and local analysts say China brings the hardware but not the capital. Keep that in mind for the Philippines, whose imports of Chinese solar more than doubled year on year in April, according to Chinese customs data.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Oras na para sa ating bokabularyo sa Tagalog. Dalawang salita ngayong umaga, parehong galing sa balita ng Pilipinas.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ang una ay pugante. Ito ang taong tumakas sa batas, may utos ng pag-aresto pero hindi mahanap, o nagtatago para hindi mahuli. Hiram ito sa Kastila, pero matagal nang bahagi ng ating pananalita, lalo na sa balita at sa korte.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Mahalaga ang pagkakaiba nito sa takas at sa nagtatago. Ang takas ay puwedeng kahit sinong nakatakas, gaya ng bilanggong tumalon sa pader, o kahit hayop na nakawala sa kulungan. Ang nagtatago naman ay paglalarawan lang ng ginagawa. Pero ang pugante ay may bigat ng batas: may kaso, may utos ng korte, at idineklara siyang wala sa kamay ng hustisya. Halimbawa: idineklarang pugante ng korte ang tatlong akusado matapos ang isang taong pagtatago.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: At pansinin ang tono. Sa pulitika, kapag tinawag mong pugante ang isang dating opisyal, matinding akusasyon iyon. Kaya maingat ang mga mamamahayag: ginagamit lang nila ito kapag may pormal nang deklarasyon.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ang ikalawa ay malabo. Sa literal na kahulugan, malabo ang hindi malinaw, gaya ng malabong tubig o malabong mata. Pero sa balita at sa usapan, ginagamit ito para sa bagay na hindi malamang mangyari. Halimbawa: malabong maabot ng gobyerno ang target sa koleksiyon ng buwis ngayong taon.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ihambing natin sa imposible. Ang imposible ay sarado na, wala nang pag-asa. Ang malabo ay may kaunting puwang pa, pero mahina ang tsansa. Mas magalang din ito: kapag sinabi mong malabo, hindi mo tahasang sinasabing hindi, kaya paborito ito ng mga ekonomista at ng mga sumasagot sa imbitasyong ayaw nilang puntahan. Malabo akong makarating, ibig sabihin, huwag mo na akong hintayin.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Pakinggan ninyo ang dalawang salitang ito sa susunod na bahagi.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Sa Sandiganbayan, idineklarang pugante ang tatlong kapwa-akusado ni dating Kinatawan Zaldy Co sa kasong may kinalaman sa 289.5 milyong pisong proyektong flood control sa Oriental Mindoro, matapos ang halos isang taong pagtatago sa kabila ng mga warrant.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Samantala, sa Bureau of Internal Revenue, umabot na sa 2.814 trilyong piso ang koleksiyon mula Enero hanggang Oktubre, pero ayon sa mga analista, malabong maabot ang buong-taong target na 3.39 trilyong piso dahil sa mahinang ekonomiya.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: On the flood-control file, the same court saw 7 public works officials from Bulacan's first district plead not guilty in a 77-million-peso Balagtas case, and Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon says about 200 flood-control cases are pending at the Ombudsman. The scandal has moved from Senate hearings to arraignments and warrants, which is slower but harder to reverse.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: On the BIR numbers, collections are up 5.63% and sit at 82.9% of the goal with 2 months left. The bureau says it will cross 3 trillion pesos by the end of November, which still leaves a gap of almost 400 billion. Tax refunds rose more than 76% to 24.1 billion. With third-quarter growth at 2.1%, a miss widens the deficit just as the peso closed Wednesday at 63.71 to the dollar. And that brings back the Bank Indonesia point: Manila faces the same choice between defending the currency and supporting growth.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Politics. Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial resumed today after the ASEAN pause, and the defense is now calling trade and food-safety officials on Cale88 Foods, the banana-chips maker 47.5% owned by her husband, Manases Carpio. Prosecutors cite at least 319 million pesos in inward remittances from China. The new detail: BPI confirmed to the court that the Vice President held US-dollar accounts.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That makes it squarely a paper trial. The defense wants Cale88 to look like an ordinary export business with ordinary foreign receipts, and the prosecution wants the dollar accounts and remittances to look like unexplained wealth. Senate President Chiz Escudero still hopes to finish in December.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And President Marcos flew straight from Wednesday's meeting with Trump to the APEC summit in Shenzhen, where he held a pull-aside with Mexico's Claudia Sheinbaum and met Vietnam's To Lam on maritime cooperation and food security. A bilateral with Xi is described as a long shot. Being in Xi's city 24 hours after hosting Trump is exactly the balancing act Manila is trying to run.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Now Mandarin, with 2 items tied to this morning's China story about Baidu.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The first is a framing structure: 对于…来说, duìyú … lái shuō, meaning for, or as far as X is concerned. It's HSK 4, and it sets up whose point of view the rest of the sentence takes. The person or thing goes in the middle. Example: 对于百度来说，AI云已经成了最重要的增长点。(For Baidu, AI cloud has become its most important source of growth.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Contrast it with 就……而言, which we taught on Monday. Both mean as far as X goes, but 就……而言 is more formal and usually narrows a topic, like 就利润而言, in terms of profit. 对于…来说 is warmer and more common, and it frames a perspective: 对于普通家庭来说，房价还是太高。(For ordinary households, home prices are still too high.) And don't confuse it with 对于 on its own, which just means regarding: 对于这个问题, on this question.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The second is 面临, miànlín, to face or to be confronted with. It's written, formal register, and it pairs with abstract nouns: 面临压力, facing pressure, 面临挑战, facing challenges, 面临风险, facing risks. Example: 很多中国科技公司面临新的出口限制。(Many Chinese tech companies face new export restrictions.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Contrast it with 面对. 面对 is active: you face something and deal with it, like 面对问题, facing up to a problem. 面临 is more passive, it describes being in a situation that has arrived at your door. So a company 面临 a crisis, but a good chief executive 面对 it. In casual speech you'd usually just say 遇到, to run into.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Listen for both in the China story next.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: 对于百度来说，国内广告需求疲软，AI云成了唯一的亮点，但这个新业务现在也面临美国新的出口限制。(For Baidu, domestic ad demand is weak and AI cloud has become the only bright spot, but that new business now also faces new US export restrictions.)

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The numbers: total revenue of about 30.8 billion yuan, down 1%, which Bloomberg counts as the sixth straight quarterly decline. Online marketing fell 22% to 11.9 billion yuan, while AI cloud infrastructure rose 94% to 8.2 billion and GPU cloud revenue nearly tripled. That's the two-speed economy in one company: the consumer-facing ad business shrinks with household demand, while enterprise and state-backed AI spending booms.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And then Washington added a third speed.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The US Commerce Department's new rule, published in the Federal Register today, requires licences for overseas data centers that supply significant compute to China-headquartered firms, covering inference as well as training, with 90 days for existing operators. That closes the rent-a-GPU-in-Malaysia route. Baidu fell about 6 to 7% to a record low on it, and Alibaba about 5%. Alibaba and PDD both report before the US open today, and Friday brings the loan prime rate, expected to hold at 3% for the 18th straight month. Holding rates while new-home prices are still down 2.4% from a year ago is the debt-deflation side of the story: Beijing funds the AI boom and leaves the household side to wait.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Arts and culture, and a record. Van Gogh's Châtaigniers en fleurs, chestnut trees in blossom, painted in 1890, sold at Sotheby's on Wednesday night for 190.4 million dollars with fees, a hammer of 165 million. That's a new record for the artist, well above the 117.2 million paid for Verger avec cyprès at Christie's in 2022.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The record came with an asterisk and a settlement. Hours before the sale, the consignors, the Blaquier-Arrieta family, reached a deal with the heirs of the publishers Samuel and Hedwig Fischer, who argue their family's 1936 sale was made under Nazi-era duress. Terms weren't disclosed. And the collection as a whole, 12 lots, made 412 million dollars against estimates of at least 414.5 million, with patchy bidding. So the headline is a record, but the detail is a collection that came in under its low estimate. Restitution claims now get priced into trophy sales, and buyers want them settled before the paddle goes up.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The contrast was at Phillips, the smallest of the 3 houses. Its evening sale on Tuesday made 104.4 million dollars, up 55% on last year, with 95% of lots sold. Modigliani's limestone Tête, from 1911, made 44.6 million against a 35-million high estimate, and David Hockney's 8-panel portrait from 1982 made 12.2 million. Phillips says nearly 90% of the lots had never been to auction before.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the lesson of this November: fresh material beats famous material. Collectors will pay up for something that hasn't been shopped around, and they'll get choosy about trophies with history.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the National Book Awards were handed out on Wednesday night. Fiction went to Hannah Lillith Assadi for Paradiso 17, over Edwidge Danticat and Valeria Luiselli. Nonfiction went to Abdelrahman ElGendy for Huna, his memoir of revolution and prison in Egypt. Poetry to Brenda Hillman for Still House in the Desert, translated literature to Vicente Luis Mora's Centroeuropa, translated by Rahul Bery, and young people's literature to David Levithan and Gabriel Duckels for The Fight of Our Lives, a history of AIDS in America. Salman Rushdie received the medal for distinguished contribution to American letters.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A prison memoir, an AIDS history and a medal for Rushdie. It's a year where the juries rewarded witness and free expression over formal experiment.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Op-eds. First, Raghuram Rajan in Project Syndicate, with a piece titled The Silver Lining of a Data-Center Slowdown. He argues that local and political resistance to the data-center build-out is useful, because it buys time. Slower construction keeps compute expensive, which slows the replacement of workers, lets chip and memory supply catch up, and gives safety research and US-China talks room to happen.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The steelman is strong. He's not a Luddite, he's a former IMF chief economist saying the speed of adoption is itself a policy variable, and friction in permitting is a crude but real brake. And it fits what we heard in the energy segment: 260 billion dollars of cancellations is the brake already working.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The counter-take?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A slowdown that nobody coordinates doesn't buy time evenly. China won't pause, and expensive compute concentrates AI in the few firms that can afford it, which is the opposite of what a safety-minded economist should want. And buying time only helps if the time gets used. Moratoria at the county level don't come with a safety agenda attached, they come with a zoning fight. The brake is real, but nobody is steering.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second, Ramesh Ponnuru in the Washington Post: Trump, Nvidia and the emergence of the Democratic China hawk. His argument is that the Nvidia scandal, with Jensen Huang's resignation and the stalled chip controls, has turned toughness on China into a Democratic weapon. The incoming Democratic Congress will press Trump from the hawkish side, with investigations into the H200 export approvals, and that could flip the politics of Beijing over the next 2 years.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's a sharp observation: for a decade the hawk position was owned by Republicans, and a scandal can move ownership fast. The counter is that it may be opportunistic and short-lived. Ro Khanna was openly receptive to H200 sales as recently as February, and Republican hawks like John Moolenaar already criticise the White House. An investigation isn't a policy. Watch whether Democrats propose stricter export rules, or just hold hearings about the old ones.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: To finish, One Good Thing. Cole Schmidt drives a tow truck in Whitehall, Michigan. His grandfather built a red truck by hand and later sold it to help pay for his bladder-cancer treatment. He died, and the truck was gone.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Then Cole found it listed on Facebook Marketplace and offered the seller, Robert Allor, about 1,200 dollars. Allor told him it had already been sold. Then he drove it to Cole's place himself and handed it over for free. In his words, the only thing that mattered to him was that this truck got back to them.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A grandson, a red truck, and a stranger who decided the right buyer mattered more than the price.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's The Morning Commute for Thursday, November 19. I'm Alex.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And I'm Sam. Have a good day, and we'll see you tomorrow.
